corrected_value.authors: Francis, Z., Jebanesan, A., & Inzlicht, M.
corrected_value.title: Leading us unto temptation? No evidence for an asymmetry in automatic associations between goals and temptations.

decisions.quote:
The current 
study replicated and extended the prime effect found by Francis et al. in the academic context 
to the physical activity domain.
decisions.location: Discussion, current-study prime-effect comparison to Francis2022
decisions.reason: Primary Discussion explicitly says the current study replicated and extended the prime effect found by Francis2022from academic to physical-activity context. Its own lexical-decision results report symmetric goal/temptation prime facilitation, the actual published finding of Francis, separately from Cheval2017asymmetry hypothesis already shipped2360. Under codebook conceptual replication/implicit own-result comparison, a post-hoc original-specific empirical retest is still a target; it is not mere background/methodology. Full printed reference establishes Francis/Jebanesan/Inzlicht2022Collabra, DOI10.1525/collabra.31030. Parent independently overturns categorical expert exclusion; no new model call or outcome inferred.

expert_decision_not_adopted.quote:
This study examined whether the cognitive asymmetry process would be replicated in 

the context of physical activity, using a high-powered design as in Francis et al. (2022).  
It should be noted that this study was originally designed to investigate whether 
exposure to weight stigma prevents the cognitive asymmetry process from occurring in people 
concerned about their weight. However, because we did not replicate the cognitive asymmetry 
process, this hypothesis was not testable, and only the cognitive asymmetry results are 
presented.
expert_decision_not_adopted.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The empirically retested original study is Cheval et al. (2017) (already represented by shipped row 2360, 10.1016/j.psychsport.2017.02.006), whose physical-activity primed lexical decision task, inclusion questionnaire, and mixed-effects analysis were preregistered (AsPredicted #52738) and re-run to test the hypothesized cognitive asymmetry interaction ('This pre-registered study aimed to replicate the cognitive asymmetry process in the physical activity domain found in Cheval et al. (2017)'; 'Contrary to our hypothesis that temptation-related primes should lead to faster recognition of goal-related target words, and that goal-related primes should not lead to faster recognition of temptation-related targets (asymmetrical activation pattern), the results revealed a non-significant Target x Prime interaction'). Francis et al. (2022) (10.1525/collabra.31030) is an earlier failed replication study in the academic context (testing Fishbach et al., 2003) cited for motivation, post-hoc sensitivity power analysis method (SIMR), and Discussion-section post-hoc consistency/extension of an unhypothesized main effect of Prime rather than an independently retested target.
